P1_fx_receipts.question: Can resident individuals receive foreign currency for services or digital exports? Any conversion or repatriation rule?
P1_fx_receipts.answer: Yes, for registered businesses. Residents, including individual entrepreneurs, with export or import contracts with non-residents must meet a repatriation requirement within the contract's time limits. Contracts above USD 50,000 must be registered for an account number; since 2024 compliance is checked by the State Revenue Committee. For any payment or transfer of USD 50,000 or more, the resident must disclose transaction details if the bank asks. A March 2026 NBK resolution reportedly lowered some thresholds for individuals (not captured).

P2_fcy_account.question: Can resident individuals hold a foreign-currency account locally?
P2_fcy_account.answer: Yes. Resident individuals may hold foreign bank accounts and need not notify the National Bank, because the authorised bank reports transfers to them.

L1_registration.question: Must an individual register a business to sell digital services/products? Simplest legal form?
L1_registration.answer: An individual entrepreneur (ИП) registers by filing a notification of commencement of activity with the State Revenue Committee via eGov/elicense, the E-Salyq Business app or a bank. Online filing is free and needs an electronic digital signature (EDS), an ID or passport, proof of residence and an OKED activity code. Liability is unlimited.

L3_income_tax_foreign.question: Income tax on foreign-source income for residents; rates or special regimes
L3_income_tax_foreign.answer: From 2026, under the new Tax Code, PIT is 10% on annual income up to 8,500 MCI (about KZT 33.4m) and 15% above. Tax residents are those with 183+ days in any rolling 12 months, or whose centre of vital interests is in Kazakhstan. Three special regimes remain: self-employed; simplified declaration (B2C focus, income up to about KZT 2.36bn, base rate 4%, reducible to 2% by local authorities, no VAT obligation; banned for 44 activities); and farmers.

L4_vat_gst.question: VAT/GST: rate, registration threshold, treatment of exported digital services
L4_vat_gst.answer: From 1 January 2026, VAT is 16% (up from 12%), and mandatory registration starts at 10,000 MCI of turnover (KZT 43,250,000 for 2026 per Deloitte; down from 20,000 MCI). Exports of goods and international transport are zero-rated. VAT on services depends on place-of-supply rules, and foreign suppliers of e-services to individuals pay 'Google tax' VAT. Simplified-declaration taxpayers have no VAT obligation.

W1_workarounds.question: Simple, legal routes around payment barriers for a beginner (no misrepresentation, nominees or sanctions evasion)
W1_workarounds.answer: Barriers: Stripe does not accept merchants here; Wise does not let residents hold money. Simple legal routes: (1) Sell digital products or software through a merchant of record: Paddle (software/SaaS only; each seller reviewed), Lemon Squeezy (bank payouts), Polar, Dodo Payments. The platform is the legal seller to your customers, handles card payments and consumer VAT/sales tax, and pays you out. You still declare the payouts as your income at home (see L3). (2) Sell services on Upwork, which is available here (not on its restricted list). Which withdrawal methods you get (bank, PayPal, Payoneer, etc.) depends on the country and shows in your account. (3) Creator income through the YouTube Partner Program (available here). (4) Paid apps and in-app sales through Google Play (merchant registration available here). (5) Client payments by PayPal (on PayPal's Payouts list as 'Send, receive, and withdraw'). (6) For direct clients, a bank transfer (SWIFT) into your own local account always works. Follow the local foreign-exchange rules (see P1) and keep invoices. Avoid: opening accounts with a foreign address, a relative's or friend's identity, or a VPN to look like you are elsewhere. It breaches platform terms (accounts and funds get frozen) and can break anti-money-laundering or sanctions law.
